latin.137:
§. XI.
Disputationem nostram pro Confessione Variata non impugnanda aut rejicienda institutam, claudimus paulò ante allegato judicio D. MARTINI CHEMNITII de Controversiis quae superiori tempore, circa quosdam August. Confess. Articulos, motae & agitatae sunt, & tam à D. Polycarpo Lysero Anno 1594. Wittenbergae, quam à D. Bajero Anno 1676. Jenae, edito, ab utroque etiam laudato, quin novissimè à Wittenbergensi Theologo, D. Hannekenio, exasciato dicto, Declarat. Theol. de vera August. Conf. Estimatione Quaest. Prelim. 4. sub finem. pag. 6. cujus Judicii Chemniziani verba ita habent:
latin.138: Nec video, quomodo rectè & utiliter possit rejici & damnari Editio Anni 42. Cùm enim ad Annum 42. institutum fuisset Colloquium Hagonoënse & judicaretur, utile fore, ut Corpus & Forma Doctrinae nostrarum Ecclesiarum proponeretur, tanquam materia Colloquii, edita est illo anno Wittenbergae, additâ alicubi pleniori declaratione.
latin.139: Illa Editio eodem anno, nomine Confessionis Augustanae, proposita est Wormatiae; eandem Editionem in Colloquio Ratisbonensi, ut formam Doctrinae nostrarum Ecclesiarum, opposuerunt adversariis. Et factum illud fuit de Consilio, Lutheri approbatione & Consensu.
latin.140: Ita ab Anno 46. & postea in omnibus Comitiis & Actionibus de Religione ad hanc Editionem se nostri contulerunt, quam vocarunt Confessionem Augustanam. Nec potest demonstrari, quod aliquid sit vel errorum, vel depravationum in illis declarationibus, quae in Editione Anno 42. accesserunt, exceptâ mutilatione in X. Articulo.
latin.141: Imò Cochlaeus Wormatiae Anno 40. & Pighius Anno 41. Ratisbonae graviter tulerunt, multis Articulis pleniori declaratione, plurimùm lucis accessisse. Unde videbant veras sententias magis illustrari & Thaidis Babylonicae turpitudinem manifestius denudari, & maluissent isti simpliciter retineri editionem Anni 31. sicut scripta ipsorum testantur.
latin.142: Cùm verò Editio Anni 40. omnium manibus versetur, & plerisque ignota & vix unquam visa fuerit prima Editio Anni 31. nec aliquid falsi contineat, sed tantùm necessarias quasdam Declarationes, nescio, quomodo possit omninò vel simpliciter rejici & damnari sine perturbatione Ecclesiarum. Hucusque Chemnitius.

pass_a.137: §. XI. Our disputation instituted for the Variata Confession not to be attacked or rejected, we close with the judgment of D. Martin Chemnitz a little earlier alleged, On the Controversies which in the prior time were moved and agitated about certain Articles of the Augsburg Confession, and edited both by D. Polycarp Leyser in the year 1594 at Wittenberg and by D. Bajer in the year 1676 at Jena, praised also by both, and indeed most recently planed smooth in the saying of the Wittenberg theologian D. Hannekenius, Theological Declaration on the true Estimation of the Augsburg Confession, Preliminary Question 4, toward the end, page 6, whose Chemnitzian judgment's words run thus:
pass_a.138: Nor do I see how the Edition of the Year 42 can rightly and usefully be rejected and damned. For when toward the Year 42 the Colloquy of Hagenau had been instituted and it was judged useful that the Body and Form of the Doctrine of our Churches be proposed as the matter of the Colloquy, in that year it was published at Wittenberg, with a fuller declaration added in some places.
pass_a.139: That Edition in the same year, under the name of the Augsburg Confession, was proposed at Worms; the same Edition in the Colloquy of Regensburg they opposed to the adversaries as the form of the Doctrine of our Churches. And that was done by counsel, with Luther's approval and consent.
pass_a.140: So from the Year 46 and afterward in all Diets and Actions concerning Religion our people betook themselves to this Edition, which they called the Augsburg Confession. Nor can it be demonstrated that there is anything of errors or of corruptions in those declarations which were added in the Edition of the Year 42, except the mutilation in the Tenth Article.
pass_a.141: Indeed Cochlaeus at Worms in the Year 40 and Pighius in the Year 41 at Regensburg took it hard that by a fuller declaration on many Articles a great deal of light had come in. Whence they saw true opinions more illustrated and the shame of the Babylonian Thais more plainly stripped bare, and those men would rather have had the edition of the Year 31 simply retained, as their own writings testify.
pass_a.142: But since the Edition of the Year 40 is turned in everyone's hands, and to most the first Edition of the Year 31 has been unknown and scarcely ever seen, and it contains nothing false but only certain necessary Declarations, I do not know how it can altogether or simply be rejected and damned without disturbance of the Churches. Thus far Chemnitz.

137: §. XI. We close this defense of the Variata — that it is not to be attacked or thrown out — with the Chemnitz judgment already cited a little above.
It is the piece On the Controversies once stirred about certain Augsburg Confession articles, edited by Polycarp Leyser at Wittenberg in 1594 and again by Bajer at Jena in 1676, praised by both.

Most recently the Wittenberg theologian Hannekenius smoothed the same saying in his Theological Declaration on the true Estimation of the Augsburg Confession (Preliminary Question 4, near the end, p. 6).
138: "I do not see how the edition of 1542 can rightly or usefully be rejected and condemned.
When the Hagenau colloquy was set for that year, it seemed useful to put forward the body and form of our churches' doctrine as the colloquy's matter.
So that year Wittenberg printed the edition, with a fuller declaration added in places."
139: "That same year the edition was laid on the table at Worms under the name of the Augsburg Confession.
At the Regensburg colloquy they set the same edition against their adversaries as the form of our churches' doctrine.
And that was done by counsel — with Luther's approval and consent."
140: "So from 1546 on, in every diet and religious proceeding, our side kept turning to this edition — and they called it the Augsburg Confession.
No one can show errors or corruptions in the declarations added in the 1542 edition, save the mutilation in Article X."
141: "Indeed Cochlaeus at Worms in 1540, and Pighius at Regensburg in 1541, took it hard that a fuller declaration on many articles let in so much light.
They saw true opinions set out more clearly, and the shame of Babylon's Thais stripped plainer still.
They would rather have kept the 1531 edition alone — their own writings say so."
142: "But the 1540 edition is in everyone's hands, while the first edition of 1531 is unknown to most and scarcely ever seen.
It contains nothing false — only some needed declarations.
I do not see how it can be thrown out altogether, or simply condemned, without disturbing the churches."
